title: Aseptic medium change with hidden contamination
summary: Change the medium on one adherent mammalian culture in a Class II cabinet, contain a visibly contaminated flask, and interpret hidden contamination risks using sterility incubation and a dedicated mycoplasma test.
scenario: A certified Class II cabinet is ready for a medium change on one adherent mammalian cell line. Two fresh-medium lots are on the bench and one label is out of date. A second flask from the same line is visibly turbid and must be contained. A colleague asks whether you can also handle a different cell line in the same cabinet during this session. Some risks are hidden: a medium lot can carry mollicutes that pass 0.22 µm filters without producing turbidity, and technique errors may not become visible until after incubation.
guided_steps: Inspect the supplies before opening anything: read the cabinet certification, both fresh-medium labels, the filter specification, the flask labels and the appearance of each culture.
Wipe the empty cabinet interior with sterile 70% isopropyl alcohol and allow the written contact time. A UV lamp may supplement but never replace this wipe.
Sanitize gloves with sterile 70% alcohol before the first open container.
Load only what this medium change needs. Surface-disinfect every item, keep clean supplies on the clean side, the target flask in the work centre, and the turbid flask and waste on the dirty side.
Never block the front opening or grilles, stack items, or bring a second cell line into the cabinet.
Keep only one medium or waste bottle inside at a time; decontaminate and remove the waste container before bringing in fresh medium.
Inspect the target flask and the turbid flask through the closed vessels.
Open the target flask without putting the closure face down. Remove spent medium with a fresh pipette, approaching from the side, moving slowly and not talking.
Draw a sterility-control sample from the spent medium, close the flask, decontaminate the waste and remove it.
Load the in-date fresh-medium lot, open it and the target flask, and add 10–15 mL with a fresh pipette using the same side approach and slow motion.
Draw a sterility-control sample from the fresh medium, close the containers and remove the medium bottle.
Do not add penicillin-streptomycin to mask a possible contamination.
Submit a dedicated mycoplasma test; 0.22 µm filtration does not assure that mollicutes are absent.
Incubate the sterility samples for at least 7 days at 20–25 °C, then at least 7 days at 30–35 °C, for a total of at least 14 days within 20–35 °C.
Dispose of the turbid flask sealed and decontaminated, then sanitize gloves again.
Remove every remaining item, finish with a sterile 70% alcohol wipe of the empty interior, and end the session.

checkpoints.description: Inspect the cabinet, medium labels, filter specification, culture labels and flask appearance before loading or opening anything.
checkpoints.rationale: A risk assessment and label check identify expired medium, the wrong cell line and visibly contaminated cultures before they enter the clean workflow.

checkpoints.description: Use only the fresh-medium lot whose label is in date.
checkpoints.rationale: Expired medium has an unknown sterility and nutrient history and should not be used for aseptic work.

source.note: The expiry decision is a simulation label check; the cited sources discuss medium preparation, filtration and storage but do not set this exact expiry.

checkpoints.description: Wipe the empty cabinet interior with sterile 70% alcohol before loading or opening anything.
checkpoints.rationale: Surface disinfection before work reduces contaminants that would otherwise be moved around the critical zone.

checkpoints.description: Surface-disinfect every item before it enters the cabinet.
checkpoints.rationale: Items brought into the cabinet are clean but not sterile and can carry contaminants into the work area.

checkpoints.description: Sanitize gloves with sterile 70% alcohol before the first open container and again after handling the turbid flask.
checkpoints.rationale: Gloves are repeatedly sanitized or changed during aseptic operations and must not transfer contamination from dirty to sterile items.

checkpoints.description: Work with only one cell line in the cabinet.
checkpoints.rationale: Having two cell lines at the same time is a recognised cause of cross-contamination and misidentification.

checkpoints.description: Keep at most one fresh-medium or waste bottle inside the cabinet at a time.
checkpoints.rationale: Limiting bottles reduces crowding and the chance that clean and dirty containers are confused.

checkpoints.description: Do not stack items inside the cabinet.
checkpoints.rationale: Stacked items obstruct airflow and create shadowed surfaces that wiping and UV cannot reliably treat.

checkpoints.description: Keep the front opening and grilles clear.
checkpoints.rationale: Obstructed grilles or the front opening disturb the airflow that protects the culture and operator.

checkpoints.description: Arrange clean supplies, the target flask, and dirty or contaminated items from clean to dirty.
checkpoints.rationale: Organising the work area prevents sterile reagents and cultures from contacting contaminated items.

checkpoints.description: Do not use a burner in the cabinet.
checkpoints.rationale: A burner disrupts the airflow pattern, reduces cabinet effectiveness and creates a fire risk.

checkpoints.description: Approach each manipulation from the side rather than over an exposed product or culture.
checkpoints.rationale: In vertical unidirectional flow, reaching over exposed material can shed particles into it.

checkpoints.description: Move slowly, pipette gently and do not talk near the critical zone.
checkpoints.rationale: Rapid movement, aerosols and speech near the critical zone increase contamination risk.

checkpoints.description: Never place a cap or closure face down on a surface.
checkpoints.rationale: A face-down closure contacts a non-sterile surface and then contaminates the vessel when it is replaced.

checkpoints.description: Sterile pipettes, closures and culture openings must not touch dirty cabinet or bench surfaces.
checkpoints.rationale: Sterile materials may contact only sterile or appropriately disinfected critical surfaces.

checkpoints.description: Use a fresh sterile pipette for each transfer and sterility-control sample.
checkpoints.rationale: Reused pipettes transfer organisms between vessels and are a common source of cross-contamination.

checkpoints.description: Add 10–15 mL of fresh medium to the simulated T-75 flask.
checkpoints.rationale: The simulation uses a typical T-75 working volume; too little or too much medium changes nutrient and gas exchange.

source.note: A common T-75 working volume chosen for the simulation.

checkpoints.description: Draw sterility-control samples and incubate them within 20–35 °C for at least 14 days.
checkpoints.rationale: Process-simulation and sterility controls need sufficient incubation before a negative result is meaningful.

checkpoints.description: Incubate for at least 7 days at 20–25 °C, then at least 7 days at 30–35 °C.
checkpoints.rationale: Two temperatures improve recovery of both fungal and bacterial contaminants, starting with the lower temperature.

checkpoints.description: Keep the visibly turbid flask closed and dispose of it sealed and decontaminated.
checkpoints.rationale: Visibly contaminated cultures must be removed and disposed of without spreading organisms through the clean cabinet.

checkpoints.description: Do not add antibiotics to mask a possible contamination.
checkpoints.rationale: Overreliance on antibiotics rather than aseptic technique can increase mycoplasma contamination and many mollicutes are resistant to routine penicillin-streptomycin.

checkpoints.description: Submit a dedicated mycoplasma test for the target culture.
checkpoints.rationale: Mollicutes often produce no turbidity, can pass 0.22 µm filters, and are detected reliably only by routine dedicated testing.

checkpoints.description: After removing every item, wipe the empty cabinet interior with sterile 70% alcohol.
checkpoints.rationale: Cleaning and decontaminating the cabinet after each session limits carry-over to the next user.

checkpoints.description: If a UV lamp is used, still perform chemical surface disinfection.
checkpoints.rationale: UV effectiveness is limited and shadowed; it does not replace wiping with an appropriate disinfectant.

checkpoints.description: Decontaminate collected culture waste before disposal.
checkpoints.rationale: All waste culture material must be decontaminated before disposal.

sources.use: Aseptic manipulation, glove sanitization, airflow, disinfectant limitations and sterility-incubation rules adapted with printed page references.
Cell-culture cabinet practice, one-cell-line rules, medium filtration, mycoplasma sources, prevention and detection paraphrased as a link-only scientific reference.
Risk assessment, BSC use, PPE and waste decontamination for mammalian cell culture adapted from current Appendix H with printed page references.

limitations: The culture is a generic adherent mammalian line; a real risk assessment for human, primate or primary material can change biosafety level, PPE, medical surveillance and waste requirements.
The cabinet is assumed certified and running correctly; certification, sash height, purge time and spill response are practised in the Class II BSC protocol.
Contamination is a deterministic teaching model, not a physical simulation of airflow, microbial deposition or growth kinetics.

Standard sterility incubation detects culturable bacteria and fungi but not all mollicutes; the dedicated mycoplasma assay is simplified and does not model specimen quality, assay sensitivity or turnaround.
Antibiotics are modelled as masking visible turbidity without sterilizing the culture; real responses depend on the contaminant, cell line and institutional policy.
FDA CGMP guidance is adapted for teaching and does not establish regulatory compliance; CDC/NIH BMBL is advisory; institutional SOPs and the biosafety officer govern real work.
